# Peripheral Devices

- Peripheral Devices are external hardware components connected to a computer for input, output, storage, or communication purposes.
- They are not part of the CPU or main memory but help in system operation.
- Classification of Peripheral Devices:
  - Input Devices: Used to enter data into the computer.
  - Output Devices: Used to display or present processed information.
  - Storage Devices: Used to store data and programs.
  - Communication Devices: Used for data communication between systems.
- Examples of Input Devices: Keyboard, Mouse, Scanner, Microphone, Webcam, Barcode Reader, Touch Screen.
- Examples of Output Devices: Monitor, Printer, Plotter, Speakers, Projector.
- Examples of Storage Devices: Hard Disk Drive (HDD), Solid State Drive (SSD), Pen Drive, CD/DVD, Memory Card.
- Examples of Communication Devices: Modem, Network Interface Card (NIC), Router, Switch, Wireless Adapter.
- Characteristics of Peripheral Devices:
  - Operate at slower speeds than CPU.
  - Require I/O interfaces for communication.
  - Can be input, output, storage, or communication devices.
  - Expand system functionality.
- Importance of Peripheral Devices:
  - Allow user interaction.
  - Provide permanent data storage.
  - Enable communication and networking.
  - Support multimedia applications.
  - Increase system usability.
- Advantages of Peripheral Devices:
  - Extend computer capabilities.
  - Improve productivity.
  - Facilitate communication.
  - Provide data storage.
  - Support real-time applications.
- Applications of Peripheral Devices:
  - Banking systems
  - Hospitals
  - Educational institutions
  - Industries
  - Communication networks
  - E-commerce systems
- Input-Output Organization enables communication between the CPU, memory, and peripheral devices.
- Peripheral devices require I/O interfaces for communication with the CPU.
- I/O Interface functions include data transfer, device communication, status monitoring, error handling, and synchronization between CPU and devices.

# Input-Output Interface

- An Input-Output Interface is a hardware module that provides communication between the CPU and peripheral devices.
- It handles data transfer, control signals, synchronization, and status monitoring.
- It contains data, status, and control registers.
- It supports Programmed I/O, Interrupt-Driven I/O, and DMA operations.

# Need for I/O Interface

- CPU operates much faster than peripheral devices.
- Different devices use different data formats.
- Provides synchronization between CPU and I/O devices.
- Reduces direct CPU involvement in device management.

# Functions of I/O Interface

- Data Buffering: Temporarily stores data during transfer.
- Control and Timing: Generates control signals and coordinates communication.
- Status Reporting: Indicates device status.
- Data Conversion: Converts data formats when necessary.
- Error Detection: Detects communication and transmission errors.

# Components of an I/O Interface

- Data Register: Stores data being transferred.
- Status Register: Contains device status information.
- Control Register: Stores commands sent by the CPU.

# Types of I/O Interfaces

- Parallel Interface: Transfers multiple bits simultaneously.
- Serial Interface: Transfers one bit at a time.

# I/O Interface with Programmed I/O, Interrupts, and DMA

- Programmed I/O: CPU continuously checks device status.
- Interrupt-Driven I/O: Device requests service when needed.
- DMA: Direct data transfer between memory and device.

# Advantages of I/O Interface

- Simplifies communication between CPU and devices.
- Handles speed mismatch.
- Improves system efficiency.
- Supports interrupts and DMA.
- Provides error checking and control.

# Applications

- Keyboards
- Printers
- Disk drives
- Mouse
- Network devices
- Industrial control systems
- Embedded systems

# Asynchronous Data Transfer

- Asynchronous Data Transfer is a method of transferring data between two devices that do not share a common clock signal.
- It uses control signals to ensure that data is transmitted and received correctly.
- Unlike synchronous transfer, the sender and receiver operate independently and communicate through handshaking signals.
- Need for Asynchronous Data Transfer: Different devices operate at different speeds, a common clock may not be available, and it ensures reliable communication between CPU and peripheral devices.
- It accommodates variable data transfer rates.
- The sender informs the receiver when data is ready, and the receiver acknowledges after receiving it.
- Methods of Asynchronous Data Transfer: Strobe Control Method and Handshaking Method.
- Strobe Control Method uses a strobe pulse to control data transfer.
- Handshaking Method uses two control signals: Request (REQ) and Acknowledge (ACK).
- Handshaking Method is more reliable than Strobe Control Method.
- Disadvantage of Strobe Control Method: No confirmation that data has been received successfully.
- Advantages of Handshaking Method: Reliable data transfer, no common clock required, supports devices with different speeds, and prevents data loss.
- Disadvantages of Handshaking Method: Slower than synchronous transfer, requires additional control lines, and more complex control mechanism.
- Synchronous vs Asynchronous Data Transfer: Clock Signal (Required/Not Required), Speed (Higher/Lower), Control Signals (Minimal/Request/Acknowledge), Complexity (Lower/Higher), and Reliability with Different Speeds (Moderate/High).
- Applications of Asynchronous Data Transfer: CPU and I/O communication, keyboard interfaces, serial communication, UART communication, network communication, and data exchange between devices with different operating speeds.
- Asynchronous Data Transfer uses either Strobe Control or Handshaking techniques.
- Handshaking is more reliable because it uses Request and Acknowledge signals to ensure successful data transfer.
- The sender places data on the bus, activates the Request signal, and removes data and request signal after receiving the Acknowledge signal.
- The receiver reads data, activates the Acknowledge signal, and clears the Acknowledge signal after receiving the data.

# Modes of Transfer

- Modes of Transfer refer to the methods used for transferring data between the CPU, memory, and Input/Output (I/O) devices.
- Types of Data Transfer Modes:
  - Programmed I/O (Polling)
  - Interrupt-Initiated I/O (Interrupt-Driven I/O)
  - Direct Memory Access (DMA)
- Programmed I/O:
  - Definition: CPU continuously checks the status of the I/O device until it becomes ready for data transfer.
  - Working: CPU sends a request to the device, repeatedly checks device status, and resumes execution when the device is ready.
  - Advantages: Simple implementation, low hardware cost.
  - Disadvantages: CPU remains busy waiting, wastage of processor time, low efficiency.
  - Applications: Simple embedded systems, low-speed devices.
- Interrupt-Initiated I/O:
  - Definition: Device interrupts the CPU whenever it is ready for data transfer.
  - Working: CPU executes another program, device sends an interrupt request, interrupt service routine executes, and data transfer takes place.
  - Advantages: Better CPU utilization, no busy waiting, faster response.
  - Disadvantages: More complex than Programmed I/O, interrupt handling overhead.
  - Applications: Keyboards, mouse, communication devices.
- Direct Memory Access (DMA):
  - Definition: Data is transferred directly between memory and an I/O device without continuous CPU involvement.
  - Working: CPU initializes DMA transfer, DMA controller takes control of the bus, and data transfers directly between memory and device.
  - Advantages: High-speed data transfer, minimal CPU involvement, efficient for large data blocks.
  - Disadvantages: Additional hardware required, more complex design.
  - Applications: Hard disks, SSDs, network interfaces, multimedia systems.
- Comparison of Transfer Modes:
  - CPU Involvement: Programmed I/O (Very High), Interrupt I/O (Medium), DMA (Very Low)
  - Transfer Speed: Programmed I/O (Low), Interrupt I/O (Medium), DMA (High)
  - Hardware Complexity: Programmed I/O (Low), Interrupt I/O (Medium), DMA (High)
  - CPU Utilization: Programmed I/O (Poor), Interrupt I/O (Good), DMA (Excellent)
  - Suitable For: Programmed I/O (Low-speed Devices), Interrupt I/O (Medium-speed Devices), DMA (High-speed Devices)
- Exam Point: DMA provides the highest performance due to direct data transfer between memory and I/O devices with minimal CPU involvement.

# Priority Interrupt

- A Priority Interrupt system is used to assign a priority level to each interrupt source so that the CPU services the highest-priority interrupt first.
- It ensures that important devices receive immediate attention.
- Multiple devices may request CPU service at the same time, and some devices are more critical than others.
- Priority Interrupt prevents loss of important data, improves system efficiency, and response time.

## Need for Priority Interrupt

- Multiple devices may request CPU service at the same time.
- Some devices are more critical than others.
- Prevents loss of important data.
- Improves system efficiency and response time.

## Types of Priority Interrupt

- **Software Priority Interrupt**: Priority is determined by software.
  - Advantages: Flexible implementation, easy to modify priorities.
  - Disadvantages: Slower than hardware priority, increased software overhead.
- **Hardware Priority Interrupt**: Priority is determined using hardware circuits.
  - Advantages: Faster response, suitable for real-time systems.
  - Disadvantages: More hardware required, higher implementation cost.

## Methods of Hardware Priority Interrupt

- **Daisy Chain Method**: Devices are connected in series.
  - Advantages: Simple implementation, low hardware cost.
  - Disadvantages: Fixed priority, failure of one device may affect others.
- **Parallel Priority Interrupt**: Uses priority encoder hardware.
  - Advantages: Faster than daisy chain, simultaneous interrupt handling.
  - Disadvantages: More hardware complexity.

## Interrupt Priority Levels

- Devices are assigned priority levels (e.g., Disk Controller: Highest, Network Interface: High, Keyboard: Medium, Printer: Low).

## Priority Interrupt Sequence

- Device generates interrupt request.
- CPU receives requests.
- Priority logic determines highest priority.
- CPU acknowledges selected interrupt.
- Corresponding ISR executes.
- CPU returns to interrupted program.

## Applications

- Operating Systems
- Real-Time Systems
- Network Controllers
- Disk Controllers
- Embedded Systems
- Communication Systems

# DMA

- Direct Memory Access (DMA) is a technique that allows data to be transferred directly between an I/O device and main memory without continuous involvement of the CPU.
- DMA improves system performance by reducing CPU workload during large data transfers.
- CPU is much faster than I/O devices, making continuous CPU involvement inefficient.
- Large volumes of data need efficient transfer, which DMA provides.

## Basic Concept

- Without DMA: I/O Device ↔ CPU ↔ Memory
- With DMA: I/O Device ↔ DMA Controller ↔ Memory

## DMA Controller

- A DMA Controller is a hardware unit responsible for managing data transfer between memory and I/O devices.
- Functions:
  - Generates memory addresses.
  - Controls data transfer.
  - Maintains transfer count.
  - Requests bus access.
  - Sends completion interrupt to CPU.

## Working of DMA

- CPU initializes the DMA controller by providing:
  - Starting memory address
  - Number of bytes/words to transfer
  - Direction of transfer
- DMA controller requests control of the system bus.
- CPU grants bus access.
- DMA transfers data directly between memory and I/O device.
- After transfer completion, DMA sends an interrupt to the CPU.

## DMA Transfer Modes

- 1. Burst Mode (Block Transfer): DMA transfers an entire block of data at once.
- 2. Cycle Stealing Mode: DMA transfers one word at a time, temporarily taking control of the bus from CPU.
- 3. Transparent Mode: DMA transfers data only when CPU is not using the bus.

## Advantages of DMA

- High-speed data transfer.
- Reduced CPU workload.
- Improved system efficiency.
- Better CPU utilization.
- Suitable for large data transfers.

## Disadvantages of DMA

- Requires additional hardware.
- More complex design.
- Bus contention may occur.

## Applications of DMA

- Hard Disk Drives (HDD)
- SSDs
- Network Interface Cards (NIC)
- Graphics Cards
- Audio Devices
- Multimedia Systems

## Comparison with Other I/O Techniques

- Feature: Programmed I/O, Interrupt I/O, DMA
- CPU Involvement: High, Medium, Very Low
- Speed: Low, Medium, High
- CPU Utilization: Poor, Better, Excellent
- Hardware Complexity: Low, Medium, High

# Serial Communication

- Serial Communication is a method of data transmission where data bits are sent one at a time over a single communication line or channel.
- It is widely used for communication between computers, microprocessors, microcontrollers, and peripheral devices.
- Need for Serial Communication:
  - Reduces the number of communication lines.
  - Suitable for long-distance data transmission.
  - Lower cost compared to parallel communication.
  - Simplifies wiring and hardware design.
- Basic Concept:
  - Bits are transmitted sequentially, one after another.
- Block Diagram:
  - Sender → Serial Interface → Communication Line → Serial Interface → Receiver
- Types of Serial Communication:
  - 1. Asynchronous Serial Communication:
    - Definition: Data is transmitted one character at a time without a common clock signal.
    - Format: | Start | Data Bits | Parity | Stop |
    - Advantages: Simple implementation, low cost, no clock synchronization required.
    - Disadvantages: Lower speed, additional start and stop bits increase overhead.
    - Examples: UART, RS-232
  - 2. Synchronous Serial Communication:
    - Definition: Sender and receiver share a common clock signal.
    - Format: Clock → Synchronizes transmission, Data → Sent continuously
    - Advantages: Higher speed, more efficient transmission, less overhead.
    - Disadvantages: More complex hardware, clock synchronization required.
    - Examples: SPI, I²C
- Modes of Serial Communication:
  - Simplex: Communication in only one direction.
  - Half-Duplex: Communication in both directions, but not simultaneously.
  - Full-Duplex: Communication in both directions simultaneously.
- Serial vs Parallel Communication:
  - Feature: Data Transfer, Number of Lines, Cost, Distance, Wiring Complexity, Speed
  - Comparison: Serial Communication is suitable for long-distance data transmission and has lower cost compared to parallel communication.
- Common Serial Communication Standards:
  - UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver Transmitter)
  - RS-232
  - SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface)
  - I²C (Inter-Integrated Circuit)
- Advantages of Serial Communication:
  - Requires fewer wires.
  - Lower installation cost.
  - Reliable over long distances.
  - Easy hardware implementation.
  - Suitable for networking and embedded systems.
- Disadvantages of Serial Communication:
  - Lower data transfer rate compared to parallel communication for short distances.
  - Data is transmitted sequentially.
  - Communication delay may occur at low speeds.
- Applications:
  - Computers and peripherals
  - Microcontrollers
  - Embedded systems
  - Industrial automation
  - Networking devices
  - Mobile devices
  - Communication systems
